specPoints.text: draw the main components of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (HR diagram)

primer.text: The HR diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature — with temperature running backwards, hottest on the left. Its main band is the main sequence; white dwarfs sit below it, red giants above right, red supergiants above those. Read the corners and every star class falls into place.

lessons.title: Reading the HR diagram
lessons.opening: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots luminosity on the y-axis (usually in solar units, Sun = 1) against surface temperature on the x-axis, which runs backwards — hot on the left, cool on the right. Most stars lie on the main sequence band from top left to bottom right; white dwarfs sit below it, red giants above its right end, and red supergiants directly above the giants.
keyPoints: The HR diagram plots luminosity (y-axis) against surface temperature (x-axis).
Surface temperature is plotted backwards, hottest on the left, coolest on the right.
Most stars lie on the main sequence band from top left to bottom right.
White dwarfs sit below the main sequence; red giants above its right side; red supergiants above the giants.
The hottest brightest stars are large main sequence stars; the coolest brightest are red supergiants.

low.restatement: Luminosity up the side, temperature backwards along the bottom, and a diagonal main sequence band.
low.analogy: A map of a city at night: the diagonal avenue (main sequence) carries most of the lights, with quiet side streets (white dwarfs) and a bright red district (supergiants).
low.examPointer: Draw the reversed x-axis first — forgetting the temperature inversion is the classic error.

medium.restatement: Region-by-region: band diagonal, dwarfs below-left, giants above-right, supergiants above them.
medium.analogy: A seating plan: the crowd on the diagonal, VIPs glowing above, quiet corners below.
medium.examPointer: Practise drawing the four labelled regions from memory — the spec asks you to draw the main components.

check.stem: On the HR diagram, surface temperature is plotted…

options.text: backwards, from hottest on the left to coolest on the right
options.explanation: The reversed x-axis is the diagram's famous quirk.
The temperature axis runs backwards.
Temperature is the x-axis.
Colour may decorate the axis, but temperature is plotted.

options.text: a band running from top left to bottom right where most stars lie
options.explanation: The diagonal band holds the majority of stars.

options.text: a cluster in the top right
options.explanation: Top right is the supergiant region.

options.text: a strip along the very bottom
options.explanation: The bottom strip is white dwarfs' neighbourhood.
It is a band of many stars.

check.stem: Where do white dwarfs sit on the HR diagram?

options.text: below the main sequence, slightly to the left
options.explanation: Hot but dim — low luminosity, leftward temperature.

options.text: above the main sequence on the right
options.explanation: That is the red giants' region.
Top left holds the brightest hot main sequence stars.
The centre belongs to the main sequence band.

options.text: directly above the red giants, in the cool bright corner
options.explanation: Cool (right) and bright (top) is their home.
Bottom left would be hot and dim — white dwarf territory.

options.text: on the main sequence band only
options.explanation: They sit above the band.
Nothing sits below but white dwarfs.

check.stem: Which stars are the coolest yet brightest?

options.explanation: Cool (red) and luminous (giant size) — top right.
Hot but dim.
Cool and dim — red dwarfs.

options.text: blue giants on the main sequence
options.explanation: Hot and bright, not cool.

check.stem: State the two quantities an HR diagram plots.
check.modelAnswer: Luminosity on the y-axis and surface temperature on the x-axis.

check.stem: State where most stars are found on the HR diagram.
check.modelAnswer: Most stars lie on the main sequence, the band from top left to bottom right.

check.stem: Explain why the main sequence band runs from top left to bottom right.
check.modelAnswer: Main sequence stars trade temperature against luminosity: the hottest ones are also the brightest, so they sit top-left, while cooler, dimmer ones extend the band down to the bottom right.

check.stem: A star is plotted with temperature 20,000 K and luminosity 10,000 times the Sun's. Locate its region.
check.modelAnswer: 20,000 K sits far left (hot) and a luminosity of 10⁴ sits high up (bright), so the star lands on the upper main sequence among the large hot stars.

lessons.title: Plotting stars on the HR diagram
lessons.opening: Plotting on the HR diagram is a two-step lookup: convert the star's luminosity into solar units (the Sun's luminosity is 1, so 10 000 times the Sun is 10⁴), then find the surface temperature on the reversed axis and mark the crossing point.
keyPoints: The Sun's luminosity is 1 in solar units.
A star 10 000 times the Sun's luminosity is plotted at 10⁴.
Locate the surface temperature on the reversed x-axis, then the luminosity on the y-axis.
Mark and label the plotted point where the two values cross.

low.restatement: Convert to solar units, find the reversed-axis temperature, mark the crossing.
low.analogy: Grid references: read along the bottom (temperature, backwards) then up the side (luminosity).
low.examPointer: The Sun = 1 convention turns '10 000 times the Sun' into a clean 10⁴ — show that multiplication in your working.

medium.restatement: Plotting is arithmetic plus orientation: 10⁴ solar units, 20 000 K, upper main sequence.
medium.analogy: Dropping a pin on a map: coordinates first, label afterwards.
medium.examPointer: Label the plotted star — unlabelled points lose the mark.

check.stem: A star with luminosity 100 times the Sun's is plotted at…

options.explanation: Solar units scale directly from the Sun's value of 1.
That is the Sun itself.
That is 10 000 times, not 100 times.
That is a hundredth, the wrong direction.

check.stem: The Sun's own luminosity on the HR diagram is…

options.explanation: Solar units take the Sun as the unit.
The Sun shines; its value is not zero.
That is a far brighter star.
The scale is defined by the Sun.

check.stem: To plot a star at 20 000 K, you locate that temperature…

options.text: towards the left side of the reversed temperature axis
options.explanation: Hotter sits further left.
The right end is coolest.

options.text: nowhere, as it exceeds the axis
options.explanation: 20 000 K lies within the plotted range.

options.text: halfway only if the star is red
options.explanation: Colour does not move the position.

check.stem: Star X has temperature 20 000 K and luminosity 10⁴ solar units. Its plotted point lies…

options.text: top left, among the hottest brightest main sequence stars
options.explanation: Hot (left) and bright (top) puts X in the upper main sequence.

options.text: bottom right with the red dwarfs
options.explanation: That corner is cool and dim.
Top right is the cool bright region.

options.text: bottom left with the white dwarfs
options.explanation: X is far too luminous for that region.

check.stem: A star shines 10 000 times brighter than the Sun. Its luminosity coordinate is…

options.explanation: Solar units scale straight off the Sun's value of 1.

options.text: left as a sentence in the margin
options.explanation: The axis needs a number.
Kelvin is the temperature axis, not luminosity.
No radius enters this plot.

check.stem: State the luminosity value used for the Sun on the HR diagram.
check.modelAnswer: The Sun's luminosity is 1 in solar units.

check.stem: State the luminosity coordinate of a star 10 000 times the Sun's.
Explain how the reversed temperature axis changes where hot stars are plotted.
check.modelAnswer: Because temperature runs backwards, the hottest stars land on the left of the diagram, so a hot bright star such as one at 20 000 K plots towards the top left, not the top right.

check.stem: Plot Star X: surface temperature 20 000 K, luminosity 10 000 times the Sun. Give the coordinates.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature coordinate 20 000 K on the reversed axis; luminosity coordinate 10⁴ solar units (10 000 × 1); mark and label the point.

glossary.definition: The diagonal band on the HR diagram where most stars, including the Sun, lie.
Luminosity units on the HR diagram with the Sun defined as 1.
The hot, dim region below the main sequence on the HR diagram.

workedExample.prompt: On an HR diagram, where do regions A (below the main sequence, left), B (the diagonal band), C (top right) and D (above the band's right end) lie, and where is a star of 20 000 K and 10⁴ solar luminosities plotted?
steps: Identify region A as the white dwarf stars, below and slightly left of the main sequence.
Identify region B as the main sequence band itself, from top left to bottom right.
Identify region C as the red supergiants and region D as the red giants above the band's right end.
Convert the luminosity: 10 000 × 1 = 10 000 = 10⁴ solar units, then locate 20 000 K on the reversed axis and plot the point.
workedExample.finalAnswer: A = white dwarfs, B = main sequence, C = red supergiants, D = red giants; Star X plots at 20 000 K and 10⁴ solar luminosity on the upper main sequence.
